questions.question: Consider  a  computer  with  a  4  MHz  processor.  Its  DMA  controller  can  transfer 8 bytes in 1 cycle from a device to main memory through cycle stealing at regular intervals. Which one of the following is the data transfer rate (in bits per second) of the DMA controller if 1% of the processor cycles are used for DMA?
questions.explanation:
Cycles used by DMA per second [latex]=1\%\times4\times10^6=4\times10^4[/latex].
Each cycle moves 8 bytes = 64 bits.

Rate [latex]=4\times10^4\times64=2.56\times10^6[/latex] bits/s = 25,60,000 bps

Answer: 25,60,000

questions.question:
The format of a single-precision floating-point number as per the IEEE 754 standard is:

Choose the largest floating-point number among the following options.
questions.explanation:
In IEEE 754, an exponent of all 1s (255) is reserved for [latex]\infty[/latex]/NaN.

questions.question:
Let [latex] f(x) [/latex] be a continuous function from [latex] \mathbb{R} [/latex] to [latex] \mathbb{R} [/latex] such that

Which one of the following options is the CORRECT value of [latex] \int_0^2 f(x) d x [/latex] ?

Adding both: [latex]2I=\int_0^2\big(f(x)+f(2-x)\big)dx=\int_0^2 1\,dx=2[/latex]

questions.question: Let [latex] A  [/latex] be the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph [latex]G[/latex]. Suppose [latex]A[/latex] is its own inverse. Which one of the following statements is always TRUE?
questions.explanation:

- [latex](A^2)_{ij}=0[/latex] for [latex]i\ne j[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] consistent with that.

A graph where every vertex has degree exactly 1 is a set of disjoint edges covering all vertices [latex]\text{---}[/latex] a perfect matching.

Answer: G is a perfect matching

questions.question: In the context of owner and weak entity sets in the ER (Entity-Relationship) data model, which one of the following statements is TRUE?

questions.question: Which one of the following regular expressions is equivalent to the language accepted by the DFA given below?
questions.explanation:
The start state loops on 0 and goes to the final state on 1; the final state loops on 0 and returns on 1. So the DFA accepts strings with an odd number of 1s.

[latex]0^*1(0+10^*1)^*[/latex]: [latex]0^*[/latex] stays at start, [latex]1[/latex] reaches the final state, then [latex]0[/latex] (self-loop) or [latex]10^*1[/latex] (go back and return) keeps it final. This is exactly "odd number of 1s".

Others fail on "1" (odd, accepted): [latex]0^*(10^*11)^*0^*[/latex], [latex]0^*1(010^*1)^*0^*[/latex] cannot give "111", and [latex]0(1+0^*10^*1)^*0^*[/latex] must start with 0.

Answer: [latex]0^*1(0+10^*1)^*[/latex]

questions.question:
Node X has a TCP connection open to node Y. The packets from X to Y go through an intermediate IP router R. Ethernet switch S is the first switch on the network path between X and R. Consider a packet sent from X to Y over this connection.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the destination IP and MAC addresses on this packet at the time it leaves X?

options.A: The destination IP address is the IP address of R
options.B: The destination IP address is the IP address of Y
options.C: The destination MAC address is the MAC address of S
options.D: The destination MAC address is the MAC address of Y

questions.explanation:
Recall how addresses change along the path:
- IP addresses are end-to-end: the destination IP stays the IP of Y on the whole path.
- MAC addresses are hop-by-hop: the destination MAC is that of the next IP hop, which is router R. A switch only forwards frames; it is never the destination MAC.

So the only true statement is: destination IP = IP of Y.

Answer: The destination IP address is the IP address of Y

questions.question:
Which of the following tasks is/are the responsibility/responsibilities of the memory
management unit (MMU) in a system with paging-based memory management?

options.A: Allocate a new page table for a newly created process
options.B: Translate a virtual address to a physical address using the page table
options.C: Raise a trap when a virtual address is not found in the page table
options.D: Raise a trap when a process tries to write to a page marked with read-only permission in the page table

questions.explanation:
The MMU is hardware that sits between CPU and memory. Its jobs:
- Translate virtual address [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] physical address using the page table True
- Raise a trap (page fault) when the entry is invalid / not present True
- Raise a trap when a write is attempted on a read-only page True

Allocating a page table for a new process is done by the OS (software), not the MMU.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.question: Consider a process P running on a CPU. Which one or more of the following events will always trigger a context switch by the OS that results in process P moving to a non-running state (e.g., ready, blocked)?

options.A: P makes a blocking system call to read a block of data from the disk
options.B: P tries to access a page that is in the swap space, triggering a page fault
options.C: An interrupt is raised by the disk to deliver data requested by some other process
options.D: A timer interrupt is raised by the hardware

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Blocking system call to read disk: P must wait for I/O [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] moved to blocked state [latex]\text{---}[/latex] always a context switch.
- Page fault for a page in swap space: the page must be read from disk [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P is blocked [latex]\text{---}[/latex] always a context switch.
- Disk interrupt for another process: the OS handles it and makes that process ready, but P can continue running [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not always.
- Timer interrupt: P may still have time left in its slice, or the scheduler may pick P again [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not always.

Answer: Options 1 and 2

questions.question: Which of the following file organizations is/are I/O efficient for the scan operation in DBMS?
questions.explanation:
A scan reads every record of the file.

- Heap and sorted files store records packed in consecutive pages, so each page is read once [latex]\text{---}[/latex] I/O efficient.
- Unclustered tree / hash index: following the index, records are scattered in random pages; the same page may be read many times (about one I/O per record) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not efficient for a scan.

Answer: Sorted, Heap

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the Two Phase Locking (2PL) protocol is/are TRUE?

options.B: With 2PL, a transaction always locks the data item being read or written just before every operation and always releases the lock just after the operation
options.C: With 2PL, once a lock is released on any data item inside a transaction, no more locks on any data item can be obtained inside that transaction

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- 2PL guarantees conflict serializability, so it permits only serializable schedules [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Locking just before each operation and releasing just after violates 2PL (a release followed by a new lock) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Growing phase then shrinking phase: once a lock is released, no new lock can be acquired [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (definition).
- Deadlock is possible: T1 locks A, T2 locks B, then each waits for the other [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1, 3 and 4

questions.question: Which of the following statements about IPv4 fragmentation is/are TRUE?

options.A: The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed only at the source of the datagram
options.B: The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed at any IP router which finds that the size of the datagram to be transmitted exceeds the MTU
options.C: The reassembly of fragments is performed only at the destination of the datagram
options.D: The reassembly of fragments is performed at all intermediate routers along the path from the source to the destination

questions.explanation:
Recall the IPv4 fragmentation rules:
- In IPv4, any router whose outgoing link MTU is smaller than the datagram can fragment it (not only the source).
- Fragments may take different routes, so reassembly is done only at the destination.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.A: An attribute grammar is a syntax-directed definition (SDD) in which the functions in the semantic rules have no side effects
options.B: The attributes in a L-attributed definition cannot always be evaluated in a depth- first order
options.C: Synthesized attributes can be evaluated by a bottom-up parser as the input is parsed
options.D: All  L-attributed  definitions  based  on  LR(1)  grammar  can  be  evaluated  using  a bottom-up parsing strategy

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- An attribute grammar is an SDD whose semantic rules have no side effects [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (definition).
- "L-attributed definitions cannot always be evaluated in depth-first order" [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE. Every L-attributed definition can be evaluated by a left-to-right depth-first traversal; that is why they are called L-attributed.
- Synthesized attributes can be evaluated by a bottom-up parser during reductions [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "All L-attributed definitions based on LR(1) grammars can be evaluated bottom-up" [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE. The marker non-terminal method is guaranteed only for L-attributed definitions on LL(1) grammars; adding markers can make an LR(1) grammar non-LR.

Answer: Options 2 and 4

Consider the following sequence of instructions to be executed in a pipelined processor:

I1: DIV R3, R1, R2
I2: SUB R5, R3, R4
I3: ADD R3, R5, R6

options.B: There is a WAR dependency on R3 between I1 and I3

The tree [latex]T[/latex] follows the convention that, at each node, all values stored in the left subtree of the node are smaller than the value stored at the node. You are not aware of the sequence in which these values were inserted into [latex]T[/latex], and you do not have access to [latex]T[/latex].
Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: Inorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]
options.B: Root node of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]
options.C: Preorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]
options.D: Postorder traversal of [latex]T[/latex] can be determined from [latex]V[/latex]

Root, preorder and postorder depend on the insertion order. Example V = {1, 2}: inserting 1 then 2 gives root 1; inserting 2 then 1 gives root 2.

questions.question:
Consider the following context-free grammar where the start symbol is [latex] S [/latex] and the set of terminals is [latex] \{a, b, c, d\} [/latex].

[latex] \begin{aligned} & S \rightarrow A a A b \mid B b B a \\ & A \rightarrow c S \mid \epsilon \\ & B \rightarrow d S \mid \epsilon \end{aligned} [/latex]

The following is a partially-filled LL(1) parsing table.

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline & a & b & c & d & \$ \\ \hline S & S \rightarrow A a A b & S \rightarrow B b B a & (1) & (2) & \\ \hline A & A \rightarrow \epsilon & (3) & A \rightarrow c S & & \\ \hline B & (4) & B \rightarrow \epsilon & & B \rightarrow d S & \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

Which one of the following options represents the CORRECT combination for the numbered cells in the parsing table?
Note: In the options, "blank" denotes that the corresponding cell is empty.

options.A: (1) [latex] S \rightarrow A a A b [/latex] (2) [latex] S \rightarrow B b B a [/latex] (3) [latex] A \rightarrow \epsilon [/latex] (4) [latex] B \rightarrow \epsilon [/latex]
options.B: (1) [latex] S \rightarrow B b B a [/latex] (2) [latex] S \rightarrow A a A b [/latex] (3) [latex] A \rightarrow \epsilon [/latex] (4) [latex] B \rightarrow \epsilon [/latex]
options.C: (1) [latex] S \rightarrow A a A b [/latex] (2) [latex] S \rightarrow B b B a [/latex] (3) blank (4) blank
options.D: (1) [latex] S \rightarrow B b B a [/latex] (2) [latex] S \rightarrow A a A b [/latex] (3) blank (4) blank

questions.explanation:
Fill the LL(1) table using FIRST and FOLLOW sets:
- [latex]FIRST(AaAb)=\{c,a\}[/latex] (A is c[latex]\ldots[/latex] or [latex]\epsilon[/latex]) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (1) [S, c] = [latex]S\rightarrow AaAb[/latex].
- [latex]FIRST(BbBa)=\{d,b\}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (2) [S, d] = [latex]S\rightarrow BbBa[/latex].
- [latex]A\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] goes under FOLLOW(A). A appears before a and before b, so [latex]FOLLOW(A)\supseteq\{a,b\}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (3) [A, b] = [latex]A\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex].

questions.question: Let [latex] x [/latex] and [latex] y [/latex] be random variables, not necessarily independent, that take real values in the interval [latex] [0,1] [/latex]. Let [latex] z=x y [/latex] and let the mean values of [latex] x, y, z [/latex] be [latex] \bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z} [/latex], respectively. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

Since [latex]0\le y\le1[/latex], we always have [latex]z=xy\le x[/latex]. Taking means: [latex]\bar z\le\bar x[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] always TRUE.

Others depend on how x and y are related:
- [latex]y=x[/latex] uniform on [0, 1]: [latex]\bar z=E[x^2]=\frac13 \gt \frac14=\bar x\bar y[/latex] (so = and [latex]\le[/latex] fail).
- [latex]y=1-x[/latex]: [latex]\bar z=\frac12-\frac13=\frac16 \lt \frac14[/latex] (so [latex]\ge[/latex] fails).

Answer: [latex]\bar z\le\bar x[/latex]

questions.question:
The relation schema, Person(pid,city), describes the city of residence for every person uniquely identified by pid. The following relational algebra operators are available: selection, projection, cross product, and rename.

To find the list of cities where at least 3 persons reside, using the above operators, the minimum number of cross product operations that must be used is

Without aggregation, "at least 3 persons in a city" means finding 3 different pids with the same city. That needs 3 copies of Person in one tuple:

[latex]\pi_{P1.city}\big(\sigma_{cond}(P1\times P2\times P3)\big)[/latex]
cond: P1.city = P2.city = P3.city and P1.pid, P2.pid, P3.pid all different.

Joining 3 copies needs 2 cross products; with only one cross product we can compare just 2 tuples.

Answer: 2

questions.question: Let [latex]A[/latex]  be an [latex] n \times n[/latex]  matrix over the set of all real numbers [latex]R[/latex]. Let [latex]B[/latex]  be a matrix obtained from [latex]A[/latex] by swapping two rows. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

questions.question:
Consider 4-variable functions [latex] f 1, f 2, f 3, f 4 [/latex] expressed in sum-of-minterms form as given below.
[latex] \begin{aligned} & f 1=\sum(0,2,3,5,7,8,11,13) \\ & f 2=\sum(1,3,5,7,11,13,15) \\ & f 3=\sum(0,1,4,11) \\ & f 4=\sum(0,2,6,13) \end{aligned} [/latex]


With respect to the circuit given above, which of the following options is/are CORRECT?

Compute the AND, OR and XOR outputs as minterm sets:
- AND: [latex]f_1\cdot f_2[/latex] = common minterms = [latex]\{3,5,7,11,13\}[/latex]
- OR: [latex]f_3+f_4=\{0,1,4,11\}\cup\{0,2,6,13\}=\{0,1,2,4,6,11,13\}[/latex]
- XOR keeps minterms present in exactly one of them: [latex]\{3,5,7\}\cup\{0,1,2,4,6\}[/latex]; 11 and 13 are in both, so they drop.

[latex]Y=\Sigma(0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7)=\Pi(8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15)[/latex] (i.e. [latex]Y=\bar A[/latex]).

questions.question: Let [latex]G[/latex] be an undirected connected graph in which every edge has a positive integer weight.  Suppose  that  every  spanning  tree  in  [latex]G[/latex]  has  even  weight.  Which  of  the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph [latex]G[/latex] ?

options.A: All edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight
options.B: All edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight OR all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have odd weight
options.C: In each cycle [latex]G[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight
options.D: In each cycle [latex]G[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], either all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight OR all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have odd weight

questions.explanation:
Take any cycle C and two edges [latex]e,f[/latex] on it. Extend the path [latex]C-f[/latex] to a spanning tree T (it contains [latex]e[/latex], not [latex]f[/latex]). Then [latex]T'=T-e+f[/latex] is also a spanning tree.

[latex]w(T')-w(T)=w(f)-w(e)[/latex]. Both trees are even, so [latex]w(f)-w(e)[/latex] is even [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]e[/latex] and [latex]f[/latex] have the same parity. So in every cycle all edges are even or all are odd [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Counter-examples for the rest:
- Triangle with all weights 1: every spanning tree has weight 2 (even), yet edges are odd [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] options 1 and 3 FALSE.
- Path with weights 1, 1, 2: only spanning tree has weight 4, but edges are mixed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] option 2 FALSE.

Answer: In each cycle, either all edges have even weight OR all edges have odd weight

Let [latex] I_0=\operatorname{CLOSURE}\left(\left\{S^{\prime} \rightarrow \bullet S\right\}\right) [/latex]. The number of items in the set [latex] \operatorname{GOTO}\left(I_0, S\right) [/latex] is ____

Items of [latex]I_0[/latex] with the dot before S: [latex]S'\rightarrow\bullet S[/latex] and [latex]S\rightarrow\bullet SS[/latex]. Moving the dot:

8. [latex]A\rightarrow\bullet d\#[/latex] (from [latex]\bullet Aa[/latex])

questions.question:

How many attempts does each wizard make before coming to this conclusion, independently?

The wizards work independently, so each of them tries all 24.

questions.question:

Q: Thus, the geophysicists tend to think of the Himalayas as an active geological event rather than as a static geological feature.
R: The natural process of the cooling of this massive edifice absorbed large quantities of atmospheric carbon dioxide, altering the earth?s atmosphere and making it better suited for life.
S: Many millennia ago, a breakaway chunk of bedrock from the Antarctic Plate collided with the massive Eurasian Plate.
questions.explanation:
Follow the references between sentences:
- S starts the story: the plates collided.
- P "This fortuitous geological event" refers to the collision, which raised the rocks.
- R "this massive edifice" refers to the raised rocks and their cooling.
- Q "Thus[latex]\ldots[/latex]" gives the conclusion.

questions.question:
A cube is to be cut into 8 pieces of equal size and shape. Here, each cut should be straight and it should not stop till it reaches the other end of the cube.
The minimum number of such cuts required is
questions.explanation:
Make three cuts through the centre, one perpendicular to each axis (length, width, height). Each cut doubles the pieces: [latex]2\times2\times2=8[/latex] equal cubes.

Two straight cuts can give at most 4 such equal pieces, so 3 is the minimum.

Answer: 3
